segments.text: Petrology studies rocks — their origin, composition, and classification — building directly on mineralogy (Chapter 3) to explain how minerals combine to form the three fundamental rock types, and closing the loop back to structural geology (Chapter 4) through the rock cycle.
form from the cooling and crystallization of molten rock (magma below the surface, lava above it). Cooling rate strongly controls texture: slow cooling (deep underground, forming
rocks, e.g., granite) allows large, visible crystals to grow (coarse-grained texture), while rapid cooling (at or near the surface, forming

rocks, e.g., basalt) produces small or no visible crystals (fine-grained or glassy texture). Composition (silica content) is the other major classification axis, ranging from silica-poor, iron/magnesium-rich
rocks (light-colored, e.g., rhyolite/granite) — this same compositional spectrum directly determines the eruption style differences described in Chapter 1.
form from the accumulation and lithification (compaction and cementation) of sediment.

sedimentary rocks are classified primarily by particle size (from coarse conglomerate/breccia, through medium-grained sandstone, to fine-grained shale) — reflecting the energy of the transporting agent (water, wind, or ice) at the time of deposition, since higher energy transports and deposits larger particles.

sedimentary rocks (such as limestone, formed from calcium carbonate, often biologically precipitated by marine organisms) form instead through precipitation from solution or accumulation of biological material rather than from pre-existing rock fragments.

blocks.text: 3. Metamorphism, metamorphic grade, and facies concepts

segments.text: transforms existing rock (of any of the three types) through heat, pressure, and/or chemically active fluids, without full melting — distinguishing it from igneous processes.

describes the intensity of metamorphic conditions (temperature and pressure) a rock has experienced, typically indicated by specific index minerals that are stable only within particular temperature/pressure ranges. A

groups together the specific mineral assemblages that form under characteristic combinations of temperature and pressure, regardless of the original (parent) rock’s exact composition — allowing metamorphic conditions to be inferred directly from the minerals actually observed in a metamorphosed rock.

(grain size, shape, and arrangement) is a critical clue to a rock’s formation conditions across all three rock types: in igneous rocks, texture indicates cooling rate (point 1); in sedimentary rocks, grain size and sorting indicate transport energy and distance (point 2); in metamorphic rocks, a distinctive

(a planar alignment of platy or elongated minerals, produced by directed pressure during metamorphism) indicates the rock formed under significant differential stress, while its absence (non-foliated texture) suggests more uniform (non-directed) pressure conditions.

describes the continuous transformation among the three rock types over geological time: igneous rock can weather and erode into sediment (forming sedimentary rock), any rock type can be subjected to heat and pressure (forming metamorphic rock), and any rock type can melt (forming new magma, and eventually new igneous rock) — illustrating that no rock type is a permanent geological endpoint. Practical field and petrographic (thin-section, microscope-based) identification combines all the tools developed across this chapter and Chapter 3: composition (from mineral content), texture (from grain characteristics), and structural context (from field relationships) together allow a specific rock to be classified and, further, its formation history to be reconstructed.

items.text: Igneous rock texture (coarse vs. fine-grained) reflects cooling rate, while composition (mafic to felsic) reflects silica content — the same spectrum that determines eruption style.

Clastic sedimentary rocks are classified by particle size (reflecting transport energy); chemical/biochemical sedimentary rocks form by precipitation or biological accumulation rather than from rock fragments.
Metamorphic grade and facies describe, respectively, the intensity and specific temperature/pressure combination of metamorphic conditions, both inferable from observed mineral assemblages.
Texture is diagnostic across all three rock types: cooling rate (igneous), transport energy (sedimentary), and directed stress/foliation (metamorphic).
The rock cycle shows that no rock type is a permanent endpoint; combining composition, texture, and field context allows both classification and reconstruction of a rock’s formation history.
